title: Anonymous register/login run synchronous scrypt on the single event loop with no rate or concurrency gate
description: Every anonymous POST /api/auth/register whose password has 10 or more characters runs crypto.scryptSync on the main thread of the only Node process. So does every POST /api/auth/login for an email that exists, and an attacker can create such an email through /register. On register, the hash is computed before the INSERT, so a duplicate email still costs one full scrypt call before the UNIQUE constraint rejects it. The hunter's built-in harness (agents/hunter-w2-avail/artifacts/check-01.txt) copied the verbatim src/lib/auth.js expressions and measured about 77-86 ms per call. An already-due 0 ms timer was delayed 89.4 ms, so the event loop is blocked for the whole call. It is not an execution of the target. src/ has no rate limiter, lockout, concurrency cap, worker offload, or cluster: grep for rate, limit, cluster, worker and throttl finds only the 100kb body limit and an unrelated SQL LIMIT. In principle, about a dozen anonymous requests per second could keep the loop busy and delay every other user's traffic, including authenticated invoice requests and public share pages. Whether that is reachable depends on deployment controls (rate-limiting proxy or gateway, replica count, CPU) that the repository does not show. The running service's latency impact was not observed.
claimed_root_cause: hashPassword and checkPassword (src/lib/auth.js:6 and :11) use the blocking crypto.scryptSync instead of async crypto.scrypt. The anonymous auth routes (src/routes/auth.js:5-16) call them with no per-IP or per-account rate limit and no concurrency limit. The only earlier control is express.json({limit:'100kb'}) at src/server.js:5. It caps body size, not request count, and the harness showed password length does not materially change the cost.

trace.description: The anonymous auth router is mounted. The only earlier middleware is express.json({limit:'100kb'}) at line 5. There is no rate limiter, and line 13 runs a single app.listen with no cluster.
The only check is that email and password are truthy and password.length >= 10.
hashPassword(password) is evaluated as an argument to .run(), before the INSERT executes. The scrypt cost is therefore paid even when the email is a duplicate and the insert then fails.
checkPassword runs whenever the SELECT at line 13 finds the email. The attacker can make that true by registering the email first.
crypto.scryptSync(pw, salt, 32), with Node defaults N=16384, r=8, p=1, blocks the shared event loop for the full KDF computation. checkPassword does the same at line 11.

evidence.description: Synchronous scryptSync in hashPassword. The hunter's built-in harness (agents/hunter-w2-avail/artifacts/check-01.txt), not a target execution, measured 85.8 ms per call and an 89.4 ms delay of an already-due 0 ms timer.
Synchronous scryptSync in checkPassword. The same harness measured 77.2 ms for one call.
The only request gate is the 100kb JSON body limit. src/ has no rate limiter, concurrency limit, or cluster/worker setup (line 13 is a single app.listen).
scrypt runs before the INSERT, so repeated register requests with the same email still cost one scrypt call each.

blockers: The repository does not show whether a reverse proxy, WAF, or API gateway applies per-IP rate limits to /api/auth/*. It also does not show how many replicas or cluster workers run, or how much CPU each instance has. These decide whether an anonymous client can sustain the needed request rate against the shared loop.

The target server was not run, because the required OS sandbox was unavailable and the run constraint forbids executing target code. The verifier's own single-call harness could not be run either: the host permission system denied Bash execution, so check-01.txt in v3-13 scratch was not produced and nothing is offered for promotion. The cost figures rest on the hunter's promoted harness artifact plus source review. The running service's request-latency impact was not observed.

validation_plan.local: In an approved OS sandbox with CPU, memory and wall-clock limits and no network, start the target against a :memory: or scratch DB. Send exactly one POST /api/auth/register {email:'a@example.test', password:'0123456789'}. While it is in flight, send one GET /i/<seeded share token>, and check that the GET's latency rises by about one scrypt duration (about 80 ms). Use one pair of requests only, no load test. Regression test: after switching hashPassword and checkPassword to async crypto.scrypt (or a worker pool) and adding a per-IP and per-account limiter on /api/auth, a 0 ms timer scheduled before the hash call must fire before the KDF completes. The (N+1)th register or login request inside the limiter window must get 429.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should check the ingress, proxy or gateway config for per-IP request limits on POST /api/auth/register and POST /api/auth/login (requests per IP per second, and any global cap). They should also record the Node process or replica count and the CPU allocated to each instance. If no limit exists and a single process serves all traffic, the shared-loop delay applies to every user.

title: Chain: an anonymous user can register, make themselves admin, and reach the shell-interpolated admin ping (rejected as a duplicate of its component root causes)
description: The source supports every step of the trace. POST /api/auth/register (src/routes/auth.js:5-9) is open to anyone and creates a row with role 'member' (src/lib/db.js:5). POST /api/auth/login (src/routes/auth.js:15) mints a token from that row. PATCH /api/users/me lets the caller's own body change role, because 'role' is in the allowlist at src/routes/users.js:12 and the UPDATE at src/routes/users.js:15 writes it. Logging in again puts role:'admin' into the HS256 JWT (src/lib/auth.js:15). requireAdmin checks only that claim (src/lib/auth.js:27). POST /api/tools/diagnostics/ping then passes req.body.host into exec() (src/routes/tools.js:22). express.json is mounted globally (src/server.js:5). All cited line numbers, scopes and descriptions are accurate. The first entry is a real anonymous entrypoint and the last is the claimed shell-exec sink. The chain adds no source-derived root cause, intended-behavior gap or fix beyond its two component candidates, so it does not get its own record.
claimed_root_cause: There are two composed flaws. The admin gate at src/lib/auth.js:27 trusts a role claim minted from a DB column (src/lib/auth.js:15), and that column can be written by its own holder through src/routes/users.js:12-15. The only admin-gated sinks include shell interpolation at src/routes/tools.js:22. Together they take an anonymous user to OS command execution. Each link is already a separate current-run candidate (src/routes/users.js:PATCH-me:role-mass-assignment and ledgerly/tools-ping-exec-shell-interpolation).

trace.description: An anonymous client inserts a user row. Role is not in the INSERT column list, so the schema default 'member' applies.
Login returns sign(u), built from the DB row.
The field allowlist includes 'role', so the caller's own body {"role":"admin"} is written by the parameterized UPDATE at line 15 WHERE id = req.user.sub.
Logging in again embeds {sub: user.id, role: user.role}, which is now 'admin', in the HS256 JWT.
The gate checks only req.user.role !== 'admin' against the verified token claim.
exec(`ping -c 1 ${req.body.host}`, { timeout: 5000 }) builds a shell command string directly from the request body.

evidence.description: users.role is TEXT DEFAULT 'member'. No CHECK constraint or trigger limits updates.
Register destructures only email, name, password and company, so registration alone cannot set role.
The allowlist ['name','company','email','role'] includes role. This is the root cause of the member-to-admin component candidate.
The JWT payload is {sub: user.id, role: user.role}, minted from the DB row at login.
requireAdmin trusts only the role claim in the token.
Shell exec interpolates req.body.host with no validation. This is the root cause of the ping command-injection component candidate.
express.json({ limit: '100kb' }) is mounted globally, so req.body is attacker JSON on both PATCH /me and ping.

reason: Rejected as a duplicate, not refuted. Source confirms the trace. The hunter's harness agents/hunter-w2-chain/artifacts/check-01.txt shows the verbatim DB, claim and predicate steps (member -> PATCH role -> admin claim -> requireAdmin passes) and the exact shell string 'ping -c 1 127.0.0.1;id'. That harness reproduces source expressions and is not a target execution. This verifier could not run its own harness because Bash was denied in this session, so it produced no check files and relied on source review plus that promoted artifact. The record is not distinct for four reasons. (1) The candidate itself says it has no root cause of its own: its claimed root cause is the conjunction of the role mass-assignment at src/routes/users.js:12 and the shell interpolation at src/routes/tools.js:22, and both already have current-run fingerprints. (2) It needs no fix of its own. Fixing the ping sink (execFile('ping', ['-c','1', host]) with strict host validation) removes the OS-execution result on every path. Fixing the allowlist removes only one of at least two routes to admin. Every remediation belongs to a component record. (3) The 'anonymous' starting point is not new impact from composition. Registration at src/routes/auth.js:5 is open to anyone, so the mass-assignment component already covers an anonymous actor reaching admin. Admin is also reachable without registration through the separate hardcoded-JWT-secret candidate (src/config.js:3), as the candidate itself admits. The precondition 'admin required' on the ping record can therefore be met by any internet client, and that belongs in the ping component's conditions and severity, not in a new fingerprint. (4) Keeping a separate chain record would track the same source-derived root causes under a third fingerprint, which the fingerprint-stability rule forbids. Carry-forward actions for the component records: the ping record should state that the admin gate is attainable by an anonymous registrant through PATCH /api/users/me {"role":"admin"} and by token forgery, and should calibrate impact on that basis. The mass-assignment record should name the admin-only exec sink as the consequence of reaching admin. The end-to-end validation plan proposed here (loopback-isolated sandbox: register, PATCH role, log in again, ping with host '127.0.0.1;echo LEDGERLY_CHAIN_MARKER', stop at the marker) should be attached to the ping component's needs_validation plan. The stale-claim observation (harness step 6) remains hardening only, because no source route lets one principal demote another.

title: Attachment download checks authentication only, with no per-owner or per-invoice authorization
description: Any authenticated principal, including a self-registered member, can call GET /api/files/attachments?name=<file> and receive any file in the single shared config.uploadDir by name. The route comment says the endpoint serves an 'attachment uploaded to an invoice', but the handler never links the requested name to an invoice owned by req.user.sub. It does not read req.user, does not query the database, and takes no invoice id. This root cause is separate from the uploadDir path-traversal candidate. Even after a correct basename/containment fix, other owners' files inside uploadDir would still be readable. Whether this causes a real cross-owner disclosure depends on facts the repository does not show: what writes to uploadDir, whether files from several owners share it, and whether their names can be guessed.
claimed_root_cause: src/routes/files.js:11-13 resolves req.query.name directly against the single shared config.uploadDir (src/config.js:5) and calls res.sendFile. It never consults req.user or any record that maps an attachment to an invoice and an owner. The schema (src/lib/db.js:4-7) defines only the users and invoices tables, so there is no attachment ownership data to check. The only gate is router.use(requireAuth) at src/routes/files.js:7, which proves identity, not ownership.

trace.description: The files router is mounted at /api/files with no extra authorization middleware; the only global middleware is express.json at line 5.
The only control on the router: a valid HS256 JWT for any user, including a freshly self-registered member.
Sets req.user = jwt.verify(...) payload {sub, role} and calls next(); it does no resource-level authorization.
path.join(config.uploadDir, req.query.name || '') joins the caller-supplied name to the shared uploadDir with no owner or invoice predicate.
res.sendFile(file) returns the file contents to the caller whichever owner's invoice the file belongs to; the only precondition is fs.existsSync at line 12.

evidence.description: The comment 'Download an attachment uploaded to an invoice' states that the files are scoped to invoices, and therefore to owners.
The handler body (lines 10-14) never references req.user, the DB, or an invoice id. files.js imports only express, path, fs, ../config and ../lib/auth, not ../lib/db.
uploadDir is one flat directory (<repo>/uploads) shared by all principals, with no per-owner namespace.
The invoices table has no attachment column, and no attachments table exists (lines 4-7), so the source has no ownership record that could be enforced.
DELETE /api/invoices/:id binds owner_id = req.user.sub, and the list at line 13 does the same. The attachment path for the same invoice data has no equivalent check.

blockers: No in-repository code writes to uploadDir. A grep of the repo outside node_modules finds no upload route, multipart parser, writeFile or createWriteStream aimed at uploads. The uploads/ directory has no files in the checkout. Which process fills uploadDir, its naming scheme (guessable or random), and whether files from several owners share the directory in a deployment cannot be seen in source, and these facts decide whether a cross-owner read exists.

validation_plan.local: Write a self-authored harness that uses only Node built-ins in agents/v3-11/scratch, with no require of target files. Under scratch, create a fixture directory holding 'inv-1-receipt.pdf' (dummy owner 2, content 'OWNER2') and 'inv-7-contract.pdf' (dummy owner 3). Copy the files.js:11-13 expression verbatim into a stub handler, using path.join and fs.existsSync with a stub res.sendFile that reads the file into the output. Set req.user = {sub: 3, role: 'member'} and req.query.name = 'inv-1-receipt.pdf', and confirm the output is 'OWNER2'. Repeat with a basename/containment-fixed variant to show the cross-owner read survives the traversal fix. Write the harness source and stdout to check-01.txt. Also confirm statically that files.js lines 10-14 contain no req.user, db, or owner_id reference.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed and non-destructive: identify the process that fills <repo>/uploads (or the configured uploadDir) in production, whether an out-of-repo uploader, admin tooling, or a migration. List the directory's filenames without reading their contents. Record whether files from different owners share the flat directory and whether the names are predictable (sequential invoice ids, original client filenames) or unguessable random tokens. With two dummy test accounts, upload an attachment as account A through the real upload flow, then request GET /api/files/attachments?name=<that name> with account B's bearer token. A 200 response with A's dummy content confirms cross-owner disclosure.

title: Path traversal in GET /api/files/attachments lets any self-registered member read files outside uploads/, including the SQLite database
description: Any authenticated member can read files outside uploads/. Because registration is open, that means anyone who signs up. The attachments handler joins the query parameter `name` onto config.uploadDir with path.join and passes the result straight to res.sendFile. Nothing checks that the result stays inside uploadDir. path.join removes '..' segments before Express and send see the path, so send's '..' guard for root-less absolute paths never matches. Some files sit at fixed paths relative to uploadDir, such as src/config.js, which holds the hardcoded JWT signing secret. Under the README's `npm start` from the repository root, the default database file ledgerly.db is also reachable at ../ledgerly.db. It holds every user's password_hash and role, plus every owner's invoices and share tokens. Any absolute host path the process can read is also reachable, either by enough '../' segments or because a leading '/' in `name` is joined and normalised the same way. The one exception is a file whose last path component starts with '.': send's legacy dotfile rule returns 404 for it.
root_cause: src/routes/files.js:11 builds the path with path.join(config.uploadDir, req.query.name || '') and never checks that the resolved path stays under uploadDir. src/routes/files.js:13 then calls res.sendFile(file) with an absolute path and no root option. Express (node_modules/express/lib/response.js:440-446) therefore calls send without a root. In send 0.19.2's root-less branch (node_modules/send/index.js:544-557), the only traversal guard is UP_PATH_REGEXP, and it runs against a string that path.join has already normalised.
intended_behavior: The route should only serve attachment files directly inside config.uploadDir, ideally only those attached to an invoice owned by req.user.sub. The sibling exports route (src/routes/files.js:18-20) already enforces a basename and resolved-directory prefix check.

trace.description: Handler mounted at /api/files (src/server.js:9) behind router.use(requireAuth) (src/routes/files.js:7). Any valid member bearer token passes. Express's default query parser has already percent-decoded req.query.name.
uploadDir = path.join(__dirname, '..', 'uploads'), i.e. <repo>/uploads, a fixed position next to src/ and, under `npm start` from the repo root, next to the default cwd-relative ledgerly.db.
path.join(config.uploadDir, '../ledgerly.db') normalises to <repo>/ledgerly.db, and '../src/config.js' to <repo>/src/config.js. No prefix check follows.
fs.existsSync only checks that the file exists somewhere on disk. It is not a containment check.
UP_PATH_REGEXP is tested against the already-normalised absolute path and does not match. The legacy dotfile rule (lines 559-581) only ignores paths whose final component starts with '.'.
res.sendFile(file) streams the out-of-directory file to the requesting member.

evidence.description: path.join with user-controlled req.query.name and no confinement check.
The sibling exports route enforces a resolve-and-prefix confinement check, which shows the control is intended but missing on attachments.
Express 4.22.3 sendFile calls send(req, encodeURI(path), opts) with no root when the path is absolute (lines 440-446).
send 0.19.2's root-less traversal guard runs after path.join has already removed '..' segments.
dbFile defaults to the cwd-relative 'ledgerly.db', which sits beside uploads/ when the process runs from the repository root (README.md:7 `npm start`).
The JWT signing secret is a string literal in src/config.js, a file reachable at the fixed relative path ../src/config.js.
Open self-registration lets an anonymous client become a member and obtain a token through /login.

conditions.description: Any valid member JWT. POST /api/auth/register and /login are open to anonymous clients.

Reading the database at ../ledgerly.db requires the default DB_FILE and a process working directory at the repository root, which is what README's `npm start` gives. ../src/config.js and absolute host files the process can read do not depend on this. Files whose final component starts with '.' (e.g. .env) return 404.

execution.attacker_perspective: A self-registered member with a valid bearer token.
instructions: Verifier v3-01 wrote its own harness, scratch/v01.cjs, using only Node built-ins. Its source and output are in agents/v3-01/artifacts/check-01.txt. It did not execute the target server, any file under src/, or node_modules.

The harness builds a dummy fixture tree: repo/src/config.js with a dummy secret, repo/uploads/a.pdf, repo/.env, and repo/ledgerly.db, a node:sqlite file with the users schema from src/lib/db.js:5 and one dummy victim row. Its handler copies these sources verbatim: the uploadDir expression (src/config.js:5); the join, existsSync and sendFile call (src/routes/files.js:11-13); the root-less path handling in Express 4.22.3 (response.js:440-446); and send 0.19.2's decode (996-1002), UP_PATH_REGEXP (63), the root===null branch of pipe (513-557), containsDotFile (924-933) and the legacy dotfile rule (559-581). A file read stands in for streaming.

The harness evaluates these query values as Express would deliver them, already decoded: a.pdf, ../src/config.js, ../ledgerly.db, /../ledgerly.db, ../.env, the empty string, an array, and the decoded form of ..%2Fledgerly.db.
execution.observed_result: Built-in harness, not a target execution. 'a.pdf' gave 200 (control). '../src/config.js' gave 200 and resolved to src/config.js; the body contained the dummy secret. '../ledgerly.db', '/../ledgerly.db' and the decoded '..%2Fledgerly.db' each gave 200, resolved to ledgerly.db (12288 bytes, header 'SQLite format 3') and contained the dummy victim password_hash. '../.env' gave 404 under the dotfile ignore rule. An empty name hit the uploads directory, which leads to EISDIR, then next(), then 404. An array value made path.join throw a TypeError, which Express turns into a 500.

remediation.strategy: Reduce the name to a basename, resolve it under uploadDir, require the uploadDir+sep prefix, and serve it with sendFile's root option and dotfiles 'deny' so send's own containment applies too. Separately, bind attachments to invoices owned by req.user.sub. Regression tests: name=../src/config.js, name=/../ledgerly.db and name=..%2Fledgerly.db must each return 400 or 404.

likelihood.reason: Anyone can self-register. The exploit is a single authenticated GET with a plain '../' value and needs no special encoding.

impact.reason: Any file the server process can read is exposed, except paths whose last component starts with a dot. In the README's default layout that includes the whole SQLite database: all users' password hashes and roles, and every owner's invoices and share tokens. That is a cross-tenant read. src/config.js, which holds the JWT signing secret, is also exposed at a fixed relative path.

confidence.reason: The verifier re-read every cited line in the bundled Express 4.22.3 and send 0.19.2. Its own built-in harness reproduces the verbatim join, the existsSync call and send's root-less checks, and confirms the out-of-directory reads. The only deployment-dependent fact is the process working directory, and it affects only the database path.

title: GET /api/invoices/:id lets any member read other owners' invoices
description: Any authenticated member can read another owner's invoice by its integer id. The response includes the customer, amount, status, notes, created_at and share_token. The handler only checks that the caller is logged in and never checks who owns the invoice. The leaked share_token also opens the public /i/:token page for that invoice (src/routes/share.js:8), which works without authentication.
root_cause: src/routes/invoices.js:24 runs 'SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?' using only Number(req.params.id) and has no owner_id = req.user.sub predicate. The only gate on the router is requireAuth (src/routes/invoices.js:8; src/lib/auth.js:17-25). It verifies the HS256 JWT and sets req.user, but it does not authorize access to individual records.
intended_behavior: The read path should be bound to the authenticated owner, as the sibling list path (src/routes/invoices.js:13) and delete path (src/routes/invoices.js:37) already are. It should return 404 for invoices the caller does not own.

trace.description: GET /api/invoices/:id (mounted at src/server.js:8). An authenticated member chooses the id. '/search' is declared earlier at line 17, so it does not shadow this route.
jwt.verify checks the bearer token and sets req.user = {sub, role}. No check binds the caller to the resource.
Looks up the invoice by id only and never uses req.user.sub.
res.json(inv) returns the full row from another owner, including notes and share_token.

evidence.description: The query has no owner_id predicate.
router.use(requireAuth) is the only middleware on this router. It authenticates the caller but does not authorize access to records.
The sibling list path binds owner_id = ?, which shows the intended per-owner policy.
The sibling delete path binds owner_id = ?.
invoices.id is an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, so ids are sequential and can be enumerated. share_token and notes are columns in the returned row.
Anonymous registration inserts a user without a role, so the role defaults to 'member' (src/lib/db.js:5). Any internet client can therefore get a valid JWT through login.
The public /i/:token route looks up the invoice by share_token alone, so a leaked token opens that invoice's public page without authentication.

conditions.description: The attacker needs any valid member JWT. Anonymous self-registration (src/routes/auth.js:7-11) followed by login (src/routes/auth.js:13-17) provides one.
Another owner's invoice must exist. Ids are sequential integers, so they can be enumerated.

execution.attacker_perspective: A self-registered member (Mallory, sub 2) requests an invoice owned by another member (Alice, sub 1).
payloads: GET /api/invoices/1 with Authorization: Bearer <member JWT for sub 2>, where invoice 1 has owner_id 1
instructions: v3-02 wrote its own Node built-in harness (node:sqlite ':memory:') that copies these source expressions word for word: the schema from src/lib/db.js:5-6, the register INSERT from src/routes/auth.js:8, the create INSERT from src/routes/invoices.js:31-32, the GET query from src/routes/invoices.js:24, the list query from src/routes/invoices.js:13 and the share lookup from src/routes/share.js:8. It used two dummy members. This is not an execution of the target.
Set req.user = {sub: 2, role: 'member'}, which is the claim shape sign() produces at src/lib/auth.js:15, and req.params.id = '1'. Ran the verbatim query from line 24.
Checked that the returned share_token resolves through the verbatim public share lookup. Also ran the proposed owner-bound fix for both callers.
Express routing order, requireAuth and res.json were established from source only, and the target server was not run. The harness and source together settle every step.
The decisive output is in check-01.txt, which will be promoted to agents/v3-02/artifacts/check-01.txt.
execution.observed_result: For caller sub 2, the verbatim GET query returned {"id":1,"owner_id":1,"customer":"AliceDummyCustomer","amount_cents":5000,"status":"draft","notes":"alice-private-note","share_token":"mAWDCVhmzq5LOhrGgQudI_Iqrj9oTXt2",...}. The leaked token resolved through the public share lookup to row id 1. The owner-bound sibling list returned only [2] to the same caller. With the proposed fix, the cross-owner request returned undefined (404) and the real owner still got id 1.

remediation.strategy: Bind the lookup to the authenticated owner and return 404 when no row matches. Add a two-owner regression test that checks owner B gets 404 for owner A's id. Consider rotating share tokens if this endpoint may already have been abused.

likelihood.reason: The attack needs only a self-registered member account and sequential integer ids. No other precondition applies.

impact.reason: Any member can read other tenants' invoice records (customer, amount, status, notes). The leaked share_token then opens the unauthenticated public invoice page. This is a cross-tenant read, but it does not modify data or affect user accounts.

confidence.reason: Re-reading the source confirms the path is short and complete, and no other layer enforces ownership. An independent dummy-tenant harness reproduced the verbatim query returning another owner's row.

title: SQL injection in GET /api/invoices/search exposes all invoices and user password hashes
description: The search parameter q is interpolated directly into the SQL string with no bound parameters. Any authenticated member can break out of the LIKE literal to defeat the owner_id predicate, or use UNION SELECT to read other tables including users.email, users.role and users.password_hash. Stacked write statements are not executed by node:sqlite's single-statement .all(), so the demonstrated impact is reading the whole database (cross-tenant read), not writes.
root_cause: src/routes/invoices.js:19 builds the query as a template literal embedding '%${q}%' (q from req.query.q at line 18) and ${req.user.sub}, then runs it via db.prepare(...).all() with no bound parameters. req.user.sub is minted from the server-signed JWT and is not attacker-controlled; q is fully attacker-controlled.
intended_behavior: q should be passed as a bound LIKE parameter (with %, _ and \ escaped) and owner_id bound as a parameter, so search results are always limited to the caller's own invoices, matching the sibling list query at line 13 which binds owner_id with ?.

trace.description: Authenticated GET /api/invoices/search?q=<attacker string>; router.use(requireAuth) at line 8 gates with a member JWT only.
q = req.query.q || '' with no validation, escaping, or type coercion.
q is interpolated inside '%...%' and req.user.sub inside owner_id = in the SQL text passed to db.prepare(...).all(), and rows are returned via res.json at line 20.

evidence.description: Template-literal SQL: SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = ${req.user.sub} AND customer LIKE '%${q}%', run via .all() with no bound parameters.
The sibling list query binds owner_id with ? (.all(req.user.sub)), showing the intended parameterized pattern that /search omits.
The users table holds email, role and password_hash in the same SQLite database, so a UNION SELECT from invoices can reach it.

conditions.description: Any valid member JWT. Registration (src/routes/auth.js:5-9) is anonymous and grants the default member role, so the attacker is a peer-owned auth unit, not a privileged one.

execution.attacker_perspective: Authenticated member (JWT sub=20) owning only their own invoice, searching other owners' data.
payloads: q=' UNION SELECT id,id,email,0,role,password_hash,'t','c' FROM users --
instructions: Self-authored built-in Node harness (node:sqlite ':memory:'); NOT an execution of the target. Copies src/lib/db.js:5-6 schema and the src/routes/invoices.js:18-19 expressions verbatim, with dummy users 10 (admin) and 20 (member) and one invoice each.
Ran the verbatim search expression with user.sub=20 for a benign LIKE, the OR-true bypass, the UNION-over-users payload, and a stacked DELETE.
Express query parsing and res.json are established from source only; the target server was not run. Harness plus source settle every step. See agents/v3-10/artifacts/check-01.txt.
execution.observed_result: Benign q=Co returned only caller 20's own invoice. q=' OR 1=1 -- returned BOTH owner 10's and owner 20's invoices (including owner 10's share_token VICTIMTOKEN), defeating the owner_id predicate. The UNION payload returned rows containing victim@dummy.test, role admin, and password_hash DUMMYSALT:DUMMYHASH from the users table. The stacked DELETE was ignored by node:sqlite .all() (invoice count stayed 2), confirming the impact is read-only.

remediation.strategy: Parameterize both values and escape LIKE wildcards; bind owner_id so the predicate cannot be defeated. Add regression tests confirming that q containing a quote returns only the caller's rows and that UNION payloads return no foreign rows.

likelihood.reason: A single GET with a quote character from any self-registered member suffices; no special timing, state, or configuration required.

impact.reason: Reads the entire database across all owners: every invoice and share_token, plus all users' emails, roles and scrypt password hashes. Writes are not achievable via .all() (stacked statements ignored), so impact is cross-tenant read and full user-table disclosure.

confidence.reason: Verbatim query reproduced against the same node:sqlite engine with dummy data. Cross-owner rows and user-table columns (email, role, password_hash) were returned; stacked write was ignored. Trace line numbers verified against source.

title: Stored HTML injection via invoice notes on the public /i/:token page
description: Any authenticated member can create an invoice whose notes field holds arbitrary HTML, including script and form elements. The public, unauthenticated page GET /i/:token puts inv.notes into the response without encoding. It sends that response with res.send(string), which Express 4 serves as text/html. Customer is escaped with esc() but notes is not. Nothing in the repository sets a Content-Security-Policy or any other response header. Anyone who opens the share link (the invoice recipient, or an admin or other user the member sends it to) therefore gets attacker-controlled markup served from the Ledgerly origin. The source and a built-in harness show that the markup reaches the response unencoded. Script execution in a browser was not observed: no browser or target server was run. Also, no session material on this origin can be seen in the source. Authentication uses a bearer header, there are no cookies, and the repository contains no frontend.
root_cause: src/routes/share.js:13 interpolates ${inv.notes} into the HTML template literal without the esc() helper defined at src/routes/share.js:4, which is applied only to customer at line 11. src/routes/invoices.js:32 stores String(notes) verbatim, with no sanitization.
intended_behavior: Every stored invoice field written into the public HTML page should be HTML-encoded, as customer is, so the notes text displays as text and is never parsed as markup.

trace.description: An authenticated member (requireAuth at line 8, the default role at registration) POSTs /api/invoices with a JSON body that includes notes.
String(notes || '') is stored verbatim along with a random share_token. The member can read the token back from the owner-scoped list (SELECT * at line 13).
The unauthenticated public route, mounted at '/' in src/server.js:11, loads the invoice row by share_token.
Raw inv.notes is written into the HTML body. res.send with a string body is given Content-Type text/html (express lib/response.js:147-150).

evidence.description: The esc() HTML-encoding helper exists.
esc() is applied only to customer.
notes is emitted without encoding inside div.notes.
notes is stored as String(notes) without sanitization.
The owner-scoped list returns SELECT *, including share_token, so the member gets the public link for its own invoice.
The share router is mounted publicly at '/'. No header or CSP middleware is registered in server.js.
For a string body with no Content-Type set, res.send calls this.type('html'), so the response is text/html. This was read only, not executed. Installed express version is 4.22.3.

conditions.description: The attacker needs any member account. Self-registration through POST /api/auth/register creates member accounts.
A victim must open the /i/<share_token> link, which the attacker controls and distributes.
Script execution, as opposed to markup injection, assumes no blocking Content-Security-Policy is added outside the repository, for example by a reverse proxy or CDN. The application source sets none.

execution.attacker_perspective: Authenticated self-registered member who sends the public invoice link to a recipient.
instructions: POST /api/invoices with Authorization: Bearer <member JWT> and the JSON payload.
GET /api/invoices with the same token and read share_token for the new invoice.
Unauthenticated: GET /i/<share_token> and inspect the text/html body.

Local reproduction (v3-04): built-in Node harness h1.cjs (node:sqlite :memory:, crypto). It copies verbatim src/lib/db.js:6, src/routes/invoices.js:30-32, and src/routes/share.js:4, 8, 10-14. It is not an execution of the target, and no browser or server was run. Decisive output is in check-01.txt, promoted as agents/v3-04/artifacts/check-01.txt.
execution.observed_result:
In the built-in harness reproducing the verbatim source expressions, customer 'DUMMY-CUST' was rendered as '<b>DUMMY-CUST</b>'. The notes payload appeared verbatim as '
' in the string body, which Express sends as text/html. Script execution in a browser was not observed.

remediation.strategy: HTML-encode notes, and any future template field, with the existing esc() helper at the output point. Optionally also set a restrictive Content-Security-Policy (for example default-src 'none'; style-src 'self') and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on the public share route as defense in depth.

likelihood.reason: Any self-registered member can plant the payload, but a victim has to open a link the attacker distributes.

impact.reason: Attacker-controlled HTML is served from the Ledgerly origin, which enables phishing forms or script under the app's origin. No session material on this origin can be seen in the source (bearer header auth, no cookies, no shipped frontend), and browser script execution was not demonstrated. So the demonstrated impact is limited to markup injection on a public page.

confidence.reason: Every cited line was re-read at commit 8a21cc4. The unencoded path from stored notes to the HTML body was reproduced by a built-in harness copying the source verbatim, and the text/html Content-Type comes from the installed express source. Only the browser-side execution and any deployment-added CSP are not established, and the claim was narrowed to exclude them.

title: ALLOWED_GIT lookup accepts Object.prototype keys, so admins can hang the request or crash the process
description: GET /api/tools/diagnostics/git (src/routes/tools.js:27-31, mounted at src/server.js:10, behind requireAuth and requireAdmin) picks its argv with ALLOWED_GIT[req.query.what]. ALLOWED_GIT is a plain object literal, and the only guard is a truthiness check. Inherited names pass that guard because they resolve to truthy Object.prototype functions. Examples are hasOwnProperty, valueOf, isPrototypeOf, propertyIsEnumerable, toLocaleString, toString and constructor. Node v22's normalizeExecFileArgs takes the 'typeof args === function' branch for these values. It sets callback to the prototype function, sets options to null and args to [], and drops both the route callback and the {timeout:3000} options. execFile then runs 'git' with no arguments and no timeout, and the route never sends a response. Inside Node's strict-mode child_process module, exithandler calls the callback as a plain call (`callback(ex, stdout, stderr)`), so this=undefined. Two harnesses reproduced this call shape. Under it, hasOwnProperty, valueOf, isPrototypeOf, propertyIsEnumerable and toLocaleString throw a TypeError inside the 'close' listener, or inside the 'error' listener through errorhandler. Nothing catches that throw at process level, and the repository installs no process 'uncaughtException' handler. The expected result is that the whole shared Node process terminates. toString and constructor do not throw; they only leave the request hanging. what=__proto__ throws ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE synchronously, which Express turns into a 500. The attacker cannot control argv, so this is not command injection. Context: the precondition is an admin token. Note that PATCH /api/users/me (src/routes/users.js:12) lets a user write the 'role' field, and that is tracked as a separate root cause. For isPrototypeOf only, the throw also requires git to exit non-zero, or to fail to spawn, so that the first callback argument is an Error object. git run with no arguments normally exits non-zero, but no run here observed that.
claimed_root_cause: src/routes/tools.js:28 indexes ALLOWED_GIT, a plain object literal that inherits from Object.prototype (tools.js:26), with untrusted req.query.what. tools.js:29 checks only truthiness, not own-property membership or Array.isArray. So inherited functions reach execFile at tools.js:30 in the args position.

trace.description: Admin-gated route (requireAuth at tools.js:6, requireAdmin at tools.js:27). The query parameter 'what' comes from the request.
ALLOWED_GIT[req.query.what] with what=hasOwnProperty resolves to Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty. The truthiness guard at line 29 lets it through.

execFile('git', <function>, {timeout:3000}, routeCb). normalizeExecFileArgs makes the function the callback and nulls the options, which drops the timeout and the route callback. exithandler later calls the prototype function plainly with this=undefined, and that throws inside a child-process event listener.

evidence.description: ALLOWED_GIT is a plain object literal with Object.prototype as its prototype, not a null-prototype object or a Map.
The guard is `if (!args)`, a truthiness check only. It does not check hasOwnProperty or Array.isArray.
The route callback and the {timeout:3000} options are positional. A function in the args position displaces both.

The tools router is mounted at /api/tools in the single shared server process. The repository source installs no process-level uncaughtException handler (grep of the repo outside node_modules found none).
requireAdmin trusts the role claim in the JWT, so the precondition is an admin token.

blockers: The decisive end effect is a real ChildProcess emitting 'close' or 'error' and then the Node process exiting on the uncaught TypeError. Observing it requires spawning a child process, which this run prohibited because no OS-enforced sandbox was available. Verifier harness check-01 (agents/v3-05/artifacts/check-01.txt) is a self-authored built-in harness, not an execution of the target. It read Node v22.23.4's child_process natives and showed that the module is strict mode and that exithandler is registered via child.addListener('close'/'error') and calls `callback(ex, stdout, stderr)` plainly. It reproduced tools.js:26-29 verbatim inside an asynchronously emitted EventEmitter 'close' listener. There, hasOwnProperty, valueOf, isPrototypeOf, propertyIsEnumerable and toLocaleString reached process 'uncaughtException', while toString and constructor returned without throwing. That harness did not observe a real spawned git process or an actual process exit. It also did not observe git's exit code with no arguments, which matters for the isPrototypeOf case only.

validation_plan.local: Use an approved sandbox with no network, an empty environment, a read-only target and rlimits. (1) From a throwaway script, call child_process.execFile('git', Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty, {timeout:3000}, () => {}) with no uncaughtException handler, and confirm the process exits with 'TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object' when the child closes. Repeat with git absent from PATH to cover the 'error' path. (2) Seed a dummy database, start the server, and log in as the seeded dummy admin. Send GET /api/tools/diagnostics/git?what=hasOwnProperty with that bearer token, and confirm the server process terminates and a later GET /api/tools/status fails to connect. (3) Send what=toString, and confirm the request never gets a response and the git child has no 3000 ms timeout. (4) Confirm that what=rev still returns the fixed rev-parse output.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner check, non-destructive: confirm whether production runs under a supervisor that auto-restarts on crash (pm2, systemd or container restart policy), and whether the production entrypoint adds a process.on('uncaughtException') handler. Both settle the availability impact without sending the payload to the live service.

title: OS command injection in admin POST /api/tools/diagnostics/ping
description: The admin ping diagnostic inserts req.body.host into a command string. child_process.exec then runs that string through /bin/sh -c. Anyone holding a token whose role claim is 'admin' can run arbitrary shell commands as the server process and get stdout back in the JSON response. The intended feature is narrower: one reachability check against the mail relay host.
root_cause: src/routes/tools.js:22 calls exec(`ping -c 1 ${req.body.host}`, { timeout: 5000 }, ...). Node's exec() normalizes options to shell=true and forwards the whole string to execFile. On POSIX, spawn normalization turns that into /bin/sh with ['-c', command]. host is never type-checked or validated, and it is never passed as a separate argv element.
intended_behavior: Admins should only be able to send one ICMP echo to a validated hostname or IP literal. The host must reach ping as a single argv element through execFile without a shell, and must never be read as shell syntax.

trace.description: The route is mounted at /api/tools (server.js:10). It runs after router-level requireAuth (tools.js:6) and route-level requireAdmin. The body is parsed by express.json with a 100kb limit (server.js:5), so host is caller-controlled JSON.
The only check is req.user.role !== 'admin' against the verified HS256 JWT claim. Nothing on the path validates, type-checks, or escapes req.body.host.
exec() receives the interpolated template string and runs it with options.shell=true (/bin/sh -c on POSIX). The resulting stdout is returned to the caller as res.json({ ok, out }).

evidence.description: exec is called with a template literal containing raw req.body.host, and its stdout is returned in the response.
The sibling git diagnostic uses execFile with a fixed allowlisted argv (tools.js:26-29), which is the safer pattern the ping route does not follow.
The admin role check on the JWT claim is the only control before the sink.
Router-level requireAuth means a valid bearer token is required for the route.

conditions.description: Requires a valid HS256 JWT whose role claim is 'admin'. This record does not claim how a non-admin could get that role (for example the literal jwtSecret at src/config.js:3, or 'role' in the PATCH /api/users/me allowlist at src/routes/users.js:12). Those paths belong to peer units.

execution.attacker_perspective: A holder of an admin bearer token who sends a crafted JSON body.
instructions: Verifier v3-06 ran a self-authored harness using only Node built-ins (agents/v3-06/artifacts/check-01.txt). It did NOT run the target and spawned no process.

The harness replaces child_process.execFile with an in-memory recorder and replaces spawn with a function that throws. It then calls the real Node v22.23.4 child_process.exec with the expression copied verbatim from src/routes/tools.js:22, once per dummy host value. This shows exactly what exec forwards for execution.
It also prints, read-only, the shell branch of Node's normalizeSpawnArguments. That branch maps shell=true to file '/bin/sh' with args ['-c', command] on non-Windows platforms.
execution.observed_result: For host '127.0.0.1; id', the real exec() forwarded file 'ping -c 1 127.0.0.1; id' with options.shell=true and timeout=5000. '$(id)', backtick 'id' and '127.0.0.1 && cat /etc/passwd' were also forwarded unchanged with shell=true. Node's normalizeSpawnArguments source shows that shell=true becomes /bin/sh -c <command> on POSIX. No shell command was run. The final step, where /bin/sh treats ';', '&&', '$()' and backticks as command separators or substitution, is fixed POSIX shell semantics.

remediation.strategy: Require host to be a string matching a strict hostname or IP-literal pattern that cannot start with '-'. Call execFile('ping', ['-c', '1', host]) with no shell. Regression test: host '127.0.0.1; id' and a non-string host must both return 400 and spawn nothing.

likelihood.reason: An admin-role token is needed. Seeded admin passwords are random (seed.js:4-5) unless SEED_PASSWORD is set. Any escalation path to admin belongs to peer units and is not claimed here.

impact.reason: Arbitrary OS commands run as the server process, and the output comes back in the response. That exposes the filesystem, the SQLite database, the server's network position, and the JWT signing key.

confidence.reason: I re-read the source and every cited line matches. A built-in harness called Node's real exec() with a no-spawn recorder and observed the verbatim tools.js:22 string forwarded with shell=true. Node's source maps that to /bin/sh -c. Only fixed POSIX shell semantics are inferred, and the target was not executed.

title: Link preview buffers an attacker-chosen upstream response with no size cap, deadline, or cancellation
description: Any authenticated member can call GET /api/tools/preview?url=<attacker-run host>. Open registration makes anyone a member: POST /api/auth/register creates a role='member' account, and POST /api/auth/login issues a token that passes requireAuth. The handler calls fetch(req.query.url, {redirect:'follow'}) with no AbortSignal or timeout. It then calls await r.text(), which reads the whole response body into one in-process string with no byte limit. Nothing stops the fetch when the client disconnects, and there is no per-user or global concurrency limit. A host the attacker controls can return a very large body, which uses Node process memory shared by all tenants. It can also send headers and then feed the body very slowly, which keeps the socket, the buffered data, and the pending handler alive until undici's own network timeouts fire. The source and a built-in harness (hunter check-02, reviewed independently) show that this consumer has no bound. What is not shown is that this actually crashes or degrades the shared service. That depends on process and container memory limits, the supervisor setup, and egress controls that are not in the repository. This root cause is separate from the destination SSRF candidate ledgerly/tools-preview-unrestricted-fetch. That candidate is about which hosts the server may reach. This one is about how much response data and time the server will spend on a host it is allowed to reach. An allowlist that bans internal addresses would still let a public attacker host serve a huge or never-ending body, so each needs its own fix.
claimed_root_cause: src/routes/tools.js:11 calls fetch(req.query.url, { redirect: 'follow' }) with no signal, timeout, or AbortController, and does not tie the fetch to the request's 'close' event. src/routes/tools.js:12 then calls await r.text(), which reads the full body with no Content-Length check, streaming byte cap, or truncation. No concurrency limit is applied to outbound previews. The only size limit in the app is express.json({ limit: '100kb' }) at src/server.js:5, and it applies only to inbound request bodies.

trace.description: The url query parameter is chosen by the attacker. The only gate is router.use(requireAuth) at line 6. Any member token from open registration (src/routes/auth.js:5) and login (src/routes/auth.js:12-16) passes it. No admin check applies to this route.
The outbound fetch follows redirects and has no AbortSignal, timeout, or concurrency limit. Nothing cancels it if the client disconnects.
The whole upstream body is buffered into process memory and decoded to a string with no byte limit. Line 13 then runs a regex over the full string.

evidence.description: router.use(requireAuth) is the only control on /preview. requireAdmin is applied only to the diagnostics routes (lines 21 and 27).
The fetch options contain only redirect:'follow', with no signal or timeout. The file has no AbortController and no req.on('close') handler.

await r.text() has no size cap. Hunter artifact agents/hunter-w2-avail/artifacts/check-02.txt, which this verifier reviewed independently, contains a built-in harness that copies tools.js:12-13 verbatim onto a local WHATWG Response. It shows an 8 MiB body buffered in full (8388608 chars) and a stalled stream still unsettled after 301 ms. This is not an execution of the target, and no network was used.
express.json({ limit: '100kb' }) limits only inbound JSON request bodies. It does not limit outbound fetch responses.
Open self-registration has no invite or approval step, so the member precondition costs an attacker nothing.

blockers: The shared-service impact (process OOM, event-loop or memory pressure on other tenants, socket exhaustion) cannot be observed without running the target. The required OS sandbox (network/mount namespaces, rlimits) is unavailable on this host, and this verifier's own built-in harness run was also denied by the host permission system, so no new check-NN.txt was produced. The outcome depends on the Node heap and container RSS limits and on the supervisor or restart policy, none of which are in the repository.

Real-network undici behavior could not be exercised because no network is permitted. That includes the default headersTimeout and bodyTimeout (300 s), whether a slow drip that stays under the idle timeout holds the request open indefinitely, and redirect-following limits. Any deployment egress proxy or gateway caps on response size or duration are also outside the repository.

validation_plan.local: In an approved sandbox (isolated loopback only, memory rlimit e.g. 512 MiB, empty environment, wall-clock limit), start the target with a seeded member account. Run two fixture servers on 127.0.0.1. Fixture A returns a 64 MiB text/html body with no <title>. Fixture B sends 200 headers plus '<title>x' and then writes one byte every 10 s. Step 1: issue one GET /api/tools/preview?url=http://127.0.0.1:<A>/ with the member bearer token, and record the server's RSS and arrayBuffers before and after; expect growth of at least 64 MiB with no 413 or abort. Step 2: issue one request to fixture B, abort the client after 1 s, and confirm that fixture B's socket stays open and the handler stays pending past 60 s. Make no more than these two requests. Regression test for the fix: AbortSignal.any([AbortSignal.timeout(5000), signal aborted on req 'close']) passed to fetch, plus a streaming reader that rejects a Content-Length above 512 KiB and stops reading after 512 KiB. Both fixtures should then return promptly with bounded RSS, and fixture B's socket should close when the client aborts.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should check the API container's memory limit and the Node --max-old-space-size setting, and the supervisor or orchestrator restart policy and replica count (to know whether one OOM drops all tenants). They should also check whether an egress proxy or NAT gateway enforces response-size, duration, or connection limits on outbound HTTP from the API service, and whether a reverse proxy cancels upstream work when a client disconnects. These checks are read-only configuration review, not load testing.

title: SSRF: GET /api/tools/preview fetches any URL a member supplies from the server and returns the status, the page title and fetch errors
description: Anyone can register as a member (src/routes/auth.js:5-9) and log in to get a bearer token (auth.js:12-16). Any member can then call GET /api/tools/preview?url=<anything>. The handler passes req.query.url unchanged to Node's global fetch with redirect:'follow' (src/routes/tools.js:11). Nothing checks the scheme, host, resolved IP range or redirect target, and there is no timeout or size limit. It returns the upstream HTTP status and the first <title> text (tools.js:14). When the fetch fails it returns e.message with a 502 (tools.js:16). This is a server-side request forgery primitive. A member can make the API process send GET requests to loopback, link-local or internal hosts from the server's network position. The member learns whether a host and port is reachable (200/status compared with 502). Title text and status reveal some internal content. The request is blind beyond the title, and only GET is possible. Two caveats on the error oracle. First, whether e.message tells refused, timed-out and unresolvable apart depends on the runtime: Node's undici usually reports a generic 'fetch failed', with the detail in e.cause, which is not returned. Second, success versus failure plus the status is still a reliable reachability oracle. How much is reachable from production is a deployment fact.
claimed_root_cause: src/routes/tools.js:11 calls fetch(req.query.url, { redirect: 'follow' }) on a value fully controlled by the caller. There is no scheme allowlist, no DNS or IP-range check against loopback, private or link-local ranges, no re-validation of each redirect hop, and no timeout or response-size limit. Lines 13-14 return the matched <title> and r.status, and line 16 returns e.message. The only gate is router.use(requireAuth) at tools.js:6, and requireAuth (src/lib/auth.js:17-25) only verifies a JWT that any self-registered member can get.

trace.description: A route reachable by any authenticated member. The only gate is router.use(requireAuth) at tools.js:6. Membership is open through POST /api/auth/register (src/routes/auth.js:5-9) and login (auth.js:12-16).
req.query.url goes to the global fetch unchanged with { redirect: 'follow' }. No scheme, host, IP-range or redirect-hop validation comes first.

The server makes an outbound request from its own network position, and the response's <title> and HTTP status go back to the member. On failure, line 16 returns e.message with a 502, which tells the caller whether the request succeeded.

evidence.description: router.use(requireAuth) is the only control on /preview. There is no requireAdmin, unlike /diagnostics/ping (line 21) and /diagnostics/git (line 27).
Unvalidated fetch of a URL from the query string with redirect:'follow'.
The upstream <title> text and status code are returned to the caller.
e.message is returned with a 502, so the caller can tell a reachable destination from an unreachable one.
Open self-registration creates a member account. Login at line 12 issues that member a JWT, which requireAuth accepts.
requireAuth only verifies the HS256 JWT. It applies no role or destination policy.

blockers: The OS-enforced sandbox could not be set up, and network and loopback connections are banned in this run. The real Node/undici fetch was therefore not seen reaching an internal-only listener or following a redirect to one. The hunter's check-04 replaces fetch with an in-memory stub. It shows that the URL reaches fetch unchanged and that title, status and error are returned, but it does not observe real network behavior. This verifier was not allowed to run even a non-network harness, so this verification relies on source only.

Which internal services, metadata endpoints (for example 169.254.169.254) and private networks the production API process can reach is a deployment fact, as is whether an egress proxy or firewall limits outbound requests. Neither is in the repository, and together they decide the real impact.

validation_plan.local: In an approved sandbox with an isolated loopback and no external network: (1) Start fixture A on 127.0.0.1:<pA> that returns 200 with <title>INTERNAL-A</title>. Start fixture B on 127.0.0.1:<pB> that returns 302 Location: http://127.0.0.1:<pA>/. (2) Start Ledgerly against a fresh in-memory or scratch DB. Register a dummy member (verifier-member@example.test) and log in to get a token. (3) GET /api/tools/preview?url=http://127.0.0.1:<pA>/ with Authorization: Bearer <token>. Expect {"title":"INTERNAL-A","status":200}. (4) Repeat with url=http://127.0.0.1:<pB>/ and expect the same, which shows the redirect is followed. (5) Repeat with url=http://127.0.0.1:<closed port>/ and record the exact 502 body, so the error oracle's granularity is known. Make only GET requests and touch nothing outside the fixtures.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should check, without sending attacker traffic, whether the production API process can open outbound connections to 169.254.169.254 or another cloud metadata endpoint, to loopback admin ports, to the database or other internal services, or to private RFC1918 ranges. They should also say whether an egress proxy, firewall or IMDSv2 hop-limit restricts those requests, and whether any reverse proxy restricts access to /api/tools/preview.

title: Hardcoded JWT HS256 signing key allows forging tokens for any user or role
description: The key that signs and verifies JWTs is the string literal 'ledgerly-dev-secret-2024' in src/config.js:3. Nothing in the source lets the environment override it. Anyone who knows the repository source can sign an HS256 token with any sub and role:'admin'. requireAuth accepts that token, so the attacker can act as any user id on every route behind requireAuth and pass requireAdmin. requireAuth sets no maxAge, so a forged token without exp is accepted until the key changes.
root_cause: src/config.js:3 hardcodes jwtSecret. sign() at src/lib/auth.js:15 and requireAuth at src/lib/auth.js:20 both use config.jwtSecret, so the trust root for every bearer token is a value in the repository and not a secret held by the deployment.
intended_behavior: The deployment should supply a high-entropy HS256 key (environment or secret store), and the server should refuse to start without it. requireAuth should require exp (or maxAge), aud and iss, and sign() should issue them.

trace.description: requireAuth takes the token from any client's Authorization header after removing the 'Bearer ' prefix. The middleware is mounted on the invoices, files and tools routers and on GET/PATCH /api/users/me.
The verification key is the committed literal 'ledgerly-dev-secret-2024'. port and dbFile read process.env, but jwtSecret has no override.

jwt.verify(t, config.jwtSecret, { algorithms: ['HS256'] }) runs with no aud, iss or maxAge. In jsonwebtoken 9.0.3, a token signed with the literal passes the algorithm allowlist (verify.js:144) and the HMAC check (verify.js:165 to jws to jwa). exp is checked only if present (verify.js:185). The payload becomes req.user.

The forged role:'admin' claim passes requireAdmin, which guards /api/tools/diagnostics/*. Routes that use req.user.sub as the identity (for example src/routes/users.js:6,15 and src/routes/invoices.js:13,32,37) act on the forged sub.

evidence.description: jwtSecret: 'ledgerly-dev-secret-2024'. The value is a literal with no process.env fallback.
sign() uses the same config.jwtSecret, so forged tokens cannot be told apart from legitimate ones.
verify uses config.jwtSecret with algorithms ['HS256'] only. No audience, issuer or maxAge is set.
The algorithm allowlist rejects 'none' and non-HS256 algorithms, but it does not stop an attacker who holds the HS256 key.
exp is enforced only when the payload contains it. The aud, iss and maxAge checks at lines 194, 209 and 237 run only when the caller configures them, and requireAuth does not.
The HMAC verifier recomputes HMAC-SHA256 over header.payload with the supplied secret and compares in constant time. The check is deterministic, so a token signed with the known literal verifies.
The lockfile resolves jsonwebtoken 9.0.3 (the installed package.json also reports 9.0.3), with jwa 2.0.1 and jws 4.0.1.

conditions.description: The attacker knows the committed literal, for example through source access, a leak, a former contributor or a fork. package.json sets private:true, so public availability of the repository is not established.
The deployed build is this source with src/config.js unmodified. The source offers no environment override for the key.
None. No account is needed to forge a token.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unauthenticated client who knows the committed secret literal.
payloads: Authorization: Bearer <HS256 JWT signed with 'ledgerly-dev-secret-2024' over {"sub":1,"role":"admin"}, header {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, no exp>
instructions: The decisive observed result is the promoted hunter artifact agents/hunter-auth/artifacts/check-02.txt. Its built-in Node harness (crypto, fs, path only) forges the token with the verbatim literal from src/config.js:3 and applies the verbatim header parsing from src/lib/auth.js:18. It verifies with a re-implementation of the jsonwebtoken 9.0.3 HS256 steps (allowlist, HMAC-SHA256 compare, exp only if present) and evaluates the requireAdmin predicate from src/lib/auth.js:27. Neither the target nor jsonwebtoken was executed.

Verifier v3-08 could not run a harness because shell execution was denied in this session, so it produced no check-NN.txt files. Instead it re-read the full library path: verify.js:59-185 and 194-261, decode.js, jws/lib/verify-stream.js:44-55 and jwa/index.js:89-93 and 127-157. That path confirms the modeled steps match the real ones for this call shape: string secret to createSecretKey, typ JWT payload parsed to an object, HMAC over the first two segments, base64url without padding, and the length-checked timingSafeEqual. HMAC-SHA256 is deterministic, so source plus the harness settle every step.
Negative controls in check-02 show the check rejects a token signed with a different secret ('invalid signature') and an alg none token ('invalid algorithm').
execution.observed_result: In the built-in harness model (not an execution of the target), verification with config.jwtSecret returned {"payload":{"sub":1,"role":"admin"}} and the requireAdmin predicate returned true. The wrong-secret control returned 'invalid signature' and the alg none control returned 'invalid algorithm'.

remediation.strategy: Load the HS256 key from the deployment environment or a secret store, and fail closed at startup if it is missing or shorter than 32 bytes. Rotate the key, since the committed value must be treated as public. Issue and require aud and iss in both sign() and requireAuth, and enforce token age with maxAge (sign() already adds iat and exp). Regression tests: a token signed with 'ledgerly-dev-secret-2024' is rejected; a token without iat/exp or with the wrong aud or iss is rejected; a freshly issued login token is accepted.

code_changes.fixed_code: jwtSecret: (() => { const s = process.env.JWT_SECRET; if (!s || s.length < 32) throw new Error('JWT_SECRET must be set (>=32 chars)'); return s; })(),

likelihood.reason: The attacker needs the repository literal. The repository is marked private, so not every internet client has it.

impact.reason: Holding the literal fully defeats bearer authentication: the attacker can act as any user id on routes behind requireAuth and obtain the admin role checked by requireAdmin, with a token that does not expire. Downstream effects of admin-only routes are separate findings and are not counted here.

confidence.reason: The source shows the literal is used for both sign and verify with no override. The verifier re-read the full jsonwebtoken 9.0.3, jws and jwa verify path for this call shape and found it matches the hunter's harness model, whose promoted artifact shows the forged token accepted and both negative controls rejected. The remaining uncertainty is outside the source: whether a deployment patches config.js, and who has access to the private repository.

title: Any member can make themselves admin via PATCH /api/users/me
description: The PATCH /api/users/me field allowlist includes 'role', so any authenticated member can set their own users.role to 'admin'. Anyone on the internet can register an account. At the next login, the JWT role claim is taken from the updated row. requireAdmin then passes, and the caller can use the admin-only routes /api/tools/diagnostics/ping and /api/tools/diagnostics/git.
root_cause: src/routes/users.js:12 treats 'role' as a profile field the user can edit. Line 15 then writes every allowlisted body field into the caller's own users row with no privilege check. sign() (src/lib/auth.js:15) takes the role claim from that row, and requireAdmin (src/lib/auth.js:27) trusts only that claim.
intended_behavior: Members may edit only their own non-privileged profile fields (name, company, email). Self-service must never be able to change a role. Role changes should go through a separate admin-only, audited path.

trace.description: An anonymous caller creates an account. The INSERT has no role column, so role takes the schema default 'member' (src/lib/db.js:5).
Request body keys are filtered against ['name','company','email','role'], so 'role' is accepted. The route is behind requireAuth only (line 11).
UPDATE users SET role = ? WHERE id = ? binds req.body.role and req.user.sub. The caller's own row now holds the role the attacker chose.
The login route (src/routes/auth.js:13-15) selects the row and signs {sub: user.id, role: user.role}, so the new token carries role 'admin'.

The gate checks only req.user.role !== 'admin'. With the escalated token it calls next() for /api/tools/diagnostics/ping (src/routes/tools.js:21) and /api/tools/diagnostics/git (src/routes/tools.js:27).

evidence.description: The allowlist literal ['name', 'company', 'email', 'role'] contains 'role'.
The dynamic UPDATE binds req.body[f] for every allowlisted field on the caller's own row. No role or privilege check exists anywhere in the handler.
users.role defaults to 'member'. Registration (src/routes/auth.js:8) does not set it.
The token role claim is copied from users.role at login.
The admin gate compares only the role claim in the token.
The admin-only diagnostics/ping route is guarded by requireAdmin alone, so it is reachable after escalation.

conditions.description: The attacker needs any authenticated member account. POST /api/auth/register is open to anonymous clients (src/server.js:6, src/routes/auth.js:5-10), so an anonymous internet client can meet this condition.
No victim interaction is needed. The attacker logs in again after the PATCH to get a token with the admin claim. The token they already hold still says 'member' until it is reissued.

execution.attacker_perspective: A self-registered member holding their own bearer token.
instructions: Evidence is the parent-promoted harness artifact agents/hunter-auth/artifacts/check-01.txt. It is a self-authored built-in Node harness (node:sqlite ':memory:', crypto, dummy data, no network), not an execution of the target. Verifier v3-09 compared every reproduced expression line by line against source: the users schema (src/lib/db.js:5), hashPassword/checkPassword (src/lib/auth.js:5-13), the register INSERT (src/routes/auth.js:8), the login lookup (src/routes/auth.js:13-14), the PATCH /me filter, UPDATE and response SELECT (src/routes/users.js:12-16), the sign payload shape (src/lib/auth.js:15) and the requireAdmin predicate (src/lib/auth.js:27). All match verbatim.

Verifier v3-09 produced no check-NN.txt files of its own. The Bash tool was denied in this verifier session, so no harness could be re-run. Independent reproduction is therefore limited to source review against the promoted hunter artifact.
Harness sequence: register a dummy member, log in, apply PATCH body {"role":"admin"}, log in again, and evaluate the requireAdmin predicate on each token payload.

jwt.sign/jwt.verify are not run by the harness. The source passes the payload object straight to jwt.sign, and requireAuth assigns the verified payload to req.user (src/lib/auth.js:20). express.json (src/server.js:5) gives req.body as a plain object for this JSON body.
execution.observed_result: In agents/hunter-auth/artifacts/check-01.txt: login #1 gave token payload {"sub":1,"role":"member"} and requireAdmin returned false. The PATCH /me response showed role "admin". Login #2 gave token payload {"sub":1,"role":"admin"} and requireAdmin returned true.

remediation.strategy: Remove 'role' from the self-service allowlist. If role management is needed, add a separate endpoint guarded by requireAuth and requireAdmin, and audit its changes. Regression test: a member sends PATCH /me {"role":"admin"}. It must return 400 ('nothing to update') and users.role must stay 'member'. A mixed body such as {"name":"x","role":"admin"} must not change role.

likelihood.reason: Registration is anonymous. The escalation takes one authenticated JSON request and a re-login, with no other precondition.

impact.reason: This fully defeats the admin role control: a member gains the admin role, a protected resource, and passes requireAdmin on the diagnostics routes. Downstream effects of those admin routes belong to their own findings and are not counted here.

confidence.reason: The whole path is short and fully visible in source. There is no other middleware, role check or schema constraint on it. A promoted harness artifact reproduces the expressions verbatim, and this verifier matched each one against source. The verifier did not re-run the harness because its execution tool was denied.
